title: Has My Shift Swap Been Approved?
observable_outcome: The learner checks whether a shift swap is approved, identifies both shift dates, and confirms which shift to work.
learning_objective: Ask whether a shift swap has been approved, identify the original and new shifts, and confirm which shift to work.

scenario.prompt: You asked to swap with Lina. Your original shift is Tuesday 6 October, 7 a.m.-3 p.m. Lina's shift is Thursday 8 October, 3 p.m.-11 p.m. The manager writes: Approved. Lina covers Tuesday morning. You work Thursday evening.
scenario.puzzle: Is the swap approved? Which shift will Lina work? Which shift will you work?
scenario.privacy_note: The workplace, names, roster, dates, and times are fictional teaching data. This activity is language practice, not employment advice.

model.status_question: Has my shift swap with Lina been approved?
model.manager_reply: Yes. Lina covers your Tuesday morning shift. You work her Thursday evening shift.
model.confirm: So Lina works Tuesday 6 October from 7 a.m., and I work Thursday 8 October from 3 p.m., right?
neutral_variants: Is my shift swap with Lina approved?
Did you approve my shift swap with Lina?

language_focus.grammar: Has my shift swap been approved? is a present-perfect passive question: has + subject + been + past participle. Is my shift swap approved? asks about its current status. Did you approve my shift swap? is active and names the decision-maker.
language_focus.meaning: The present-perfect question asks whether the approval happened before now and matters now. The readback names both dates and start times so each person knows which shift to work.
language_focus.appropriateness: Ask for status without assuming approval. After receiving an answer, confirm both people, both dates, and both start times. Use right? only as a check, not as pressure for agreement.
language_focus.pronunciation: In natural speech, has and been are often unstressed. Put stronger stress on swap, approved, Tuesday, Thursday, 7, and 3 when those details carry the contrast.
language_focus.workplace_note: Roster rules differ. Follow the actual workplace process, and do not treat a proposed swap as approved until the responsible person confirms it.

evidence_activity.prompt: Which line proves the swap is confirmed?

options.feedback: Correct. Approved gives the status, and the next words show who covers the original shift.

options.text: You asked to swap with Lina.
options.feedback: This proves a request exists. It does not prove the manager accepted it.
This identifies the old shift. It gives no approval status.

question_activity.prompt: Which question checks approval without assuming it?

options.text: Has my shift swap with Lina been approved?
options.feedback: Correct. This asks whether the decision happened and matters now.

options.text: My shift swap is approved, isn't it?
options.feedback: This expects agreement. Use an open yes-no question when the status is unknown.

options.text: Why haven't you approved my shift swap?
options.feedback: This assumes refusal or delay. First ask whether the swap has been approved.

production_task.scenario: You asked to swap with Omar. Your original shift is Saturday 10 October, 10 a.m.-6 p.m. Omar's shift is Monday 12 October, 2 p.m.-10 p.m. The manager has not answered yet.
production_task.instruction: Write one neutral status question. Then imagine the manager says yes. Write a readback naming who works each date and start time.
acceptable_responses: Has my shift swap with Omar been approved? So Omar works Saturday 10 October from 10 a.m., and I work Monday 12 October from 2 p.m., right?
Is my shift swap with Omar approved? To confirm, Omar covers Saturday at 10 a.m., and I work Monday at 2 p.m., right?
production_task.valid_variants: Has ... been approved?, Is ... approved?, and Did you approve ...? can all work. They differ in grammar and focus. A readback can use covers, works, or takes if the meaning stays clear.

review_prompt: Tomorrow, recall this sequence: ask status, identify the original shift, identify the new shift, and read both details back.

design.texture: Restrained fibres and speckles generated procedurally.
design.depth: Calendar cards, people, arrows, stamp, clocks, and speech cards use cream cut edges, overlap, and offset shadows.
design.motion_principle: Calendar cards slide onto the roster; the swap arrows cross; the approval stamp descends and rebounds; the question card unfolds; the worker cards exchange places while clock hands pivot; the transfer roster repeats the sequence.
design.accessibility: Dark navy text sits on cream panels. Every colour relationship also has names, dates, times, arrows, and shape labels.

visual.title: Ask, read, confirm
visual.alt_text: A colourful layered papercut roster path. A Tuesday 6 October 7 a.m. card and a Thursday 8 October 3 p.m. card connect through a swap request. An approval stamp leads to a status question and a readback naming Lina on Tuesday and the learner on Thursday.
visual.prose: First ask whether the swap is approved. Then identify the original shift and the new shift. Read back who works each date and start time. Approval status plus two clear assignments prevents the roster details from being confused.
